newsitem.title: UK: U.S. tobacco settlement has implications elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco settlement has implications elsewhere.

text.p: The landmark tobacco settlement reached in the United States on Friday will have far-reaching implications in other countries and will spur more cancer victims and health agencies to take action, a British lawyer predicted on Monday.

Martyn Day, who is representing 23 lung cancer sufferers in Britain's first class action suit against two tobacco companies on a no-win, no-fee basis, said the $368.6 billion U.S. case and the tobacco companies' admission that their product is addictive "has been a fantastic development for Britain and the rest of the world".

"It provides an atmosphere where, for the first time perhaps, the wall of invulnerability that the tobacco companies over 50 years have built around themselves is now totally gone. The emperor has no clothes," he said in a telephone interview.

Since the U.S. settlement was announced, Day said, he has been inundated with calls from other cancer sufferers and several regional health authorities which run Britain's national health service are considering launching legal action against the tobacco manufacturers.
"We're in the first steps of considering litigation," Andrew Davies, a spokesman for the Croydon Health Authority south of London said.
The chief executive of his area has contacted 11 other health districts to see if they are are interested in taking some sort of action.
"The British action is a result of the decision in the United States but it will be three or four weeks before we decide whether we will take litigation," he added.
Day said the fact that the health authorities are considering action is an indication of what will happen.

"I would be surprised if we didn't see a consortium of health authorities in Britain taking action against the tobacco companies...and if we didn't see the government react. Possibly legislating to take on the tobacco companies."

He believes the U.S. settlement could be particularly important for his clients who are suing Imperial Tobacco and Gallaher Group Plc, which together have 80 percent of the British market, for failing to change their product to limit the dangers of smoking.

His case is based on the claim that the tobacco companies, makers of Benson and Hedges, Silk Cut and Embassy brands, were aware in the 1950s that their products were addictive and killing large numbers of their consumers. Day alleges that they were aware that tar was the primary cause of death.
Both tobacco companies insist that the U.S. agreement has no relation on the British case and neither is considering a settlement.
"So far as tobacco litigation in the U.K. is concerned that will continue to be defended vigorously by us. It will not be settled," said Ian Birks, general manager of external affairs at Gallaher.
"We are not guided by developments in the states," he added.
Paul Sadler of Imperial Tobacco agreed that the U.S. settlement was not relevant to what is happening in Britain.
Dr Julian Fulbrook, a lecturer in law at the London School of Economics and a personal injury expert, believes the U.S. settlement has changed tobacco litigation.
"The climate has definitely changed," he said.
"This huge settlement, the largest there has ever been, puts everything else in the shade but it is difficult to predict how it is going to pan out."

Day, who has been working closely with the key negotiators involved in the American settlement, said he has written to British Health Minister Tessa Jowell requesting a meeting to discuss the prospects of litigation against the tobacco giants.

He estimates that of the 35,000 cancer victims diagnosed in Britain each year up to 20,000 of them would have a good claim which could cost the main tobacco companies up to one billion pounds ($1.6 billion) a year in damages.
